newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Poll shows NZ's Peters under pressure in home base.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows NZ's Peters under pressure in home base.

text.p: Deputy Prime Minister and Treasurer Winston Peters' New Zealand First Party is struggling in the polls, and soundings in his electorate suggest his hold on the seat may be loosening.

Peters, a former cabinet minister in the conservative National Party, launched his nationalist party in 1993 and polled almost 30 percent support this time last year after launching a campaign against foreign investment and immigration levels.
After polling 13 percent in the October 1996 election NZ First held the balance of power.

Support began to fall when it opted to form a coalition with National. Since then, major policy compromises, an alleged assault on a goverment MP by Peters and allegations of mispending by NZ First MPs have further undermined the party's position.

At the end of last week, after another round of spending allegations, Peters told an audience in his Tauranga constituency: "It has been a trying week, or another trying week, in what has been a trying year, in what is becoming a trying career."
Recent polls have put NZ First support at around five per cent - the threshold at which parties qualify for seats under New Zealand's German-style MMP electoral system.
Parties with less than five percent support must rely on winning a constituency to qualify for a percentage of the seats.
But recent polls have suggested NZ First may be in trouble in its Maori powerbase.
In 1996 the party won all five Maori constituency seats, sweeping away the traditional dominance of the Labour Party.

But a Waikato University poll released on Sunday showed Maori turning away from the party, while remaining loyal to Peters. Of those polled, 45.8 percent said they had voted for NZ First and 34 percent for Labour at the election.
Asked how they would vote if an election were held now, 49 percent said Labour and only 27.7 percent NZ First.
Significantly, 66 percent believed NZ First should be in coalition with Labour.
While Peters, of Maori and Scottish descent, remained the most popular choice for Prime Minister among Maori that will not help in his eastern North Island Tauranga seat.
It is not a Maori seat, but a general seat with a big proportion of middle class and elderly voters.
In flavour it is a National seat, but Peters' personal support returned him a majority of more than 8000 at the election.
Yet a recent poll suggests his hold on the seat is weakening.
While the bona fides of the poll can be doubted -- it was sponsored by free market party Act New Zealand but organised by a respected pollster -- it is supported by anecdotal evidence.
The poll showed NZ First support in Tauranga had dropped from 32 percent on election night to just nine percent. National was up 18 points to 44 percent.
Former National Cabinet Minister Katherine O'Regan -- squeezed out of the executive by the need to accommodate NZ First ministers -- has been running a campaign to build support.
In Wellington she is prominent in a cross-party group of women MPs opposed to Peters' push to introduce compulsory pension savings at a referendum in September.
While the list vote determines the overall level of support for a party the local constituency vote is also bad news for Peters, according to the poll.
On election night he won 50 percent of the vote. National won 29 percent.
In the Act-sponsored poll his personal support was down to 23 percent against hypothetical candidates from National, 40 percent, and Labour, 23 percent.

A day with Peters in the electorate as he opened a job training centre and a new wing at the local high school confirmed a level of disaffection with Peters, although it was among groups that traditionally would not support a centre-right government.
Two tutors at the training centre were less than pleased to see Peters, telling Reuters he would "probably close it again" given his plan to promote work for the dole schemes.
"He has moved from very positive to neutral," one of the tutors said of the view of Peters in the electorate.
One teacher at the high school said Peters' support had been damaged by the compromises of office.
"He has given up a lot to get that job (as Treasurer).
"I suppose he needs to be here after dealing to the kindergarten teachers," the teacher said, referring to a recent government decision to exclude kindergartens from state wage negotiations.
Peters delivers his first Budget in June as he tries to boost NZ First's support by pojinting to the extra spending his party has leveraged out of the coalition.
